text: Before Verre had a name, before any crown was forged or any king was laid in stone, something slept beneath the mountain, and it remembered. It kept the shape of stone, the hollow of every chamber, the weight of everything that came near it, and it let nothing go. Centuries later, the founders of House Valor broke through into the dark and found it waiting. They called it the Crownheart. The first rulers did not understand what they had found. They learned only this: it answered to blood, so they gave it theirs. Before the ancient ring, the first king opened his palm and the stone drank. Doors that were never built for human hands swung open. Hidden chambers breathed again. Preserved memories obeyed, and a promise became a belief, and the belief became law. The castle remembers its rightful king. Caer Verre rose above the Crownheart. Walls became towers, towers became halls, and generations passed beneath its banners. Every coronation deepened the binding. Every royal rite drew the castle closer to the blood. House Valor believed it owned the Crownheart's memory. It never understood that the Crownheart was learning House Valor. Under King Aldrin Valor, a long war came home at last. The fires of the siege burned from one horizon to the other. Behind the gates, the people of Verre crowded into the halls and waited for the end, but the king did not wait. By candlelight, deep in the royal archives, he searched the records of his fathers, and he found a possibility. The whole of Caer Verre held forever at one chosen moment. But the Crownheart could not hold so much without living resonance. It needed lives bound into its memory, thousands of them. Aldrin looked upon the people sheltering inside his walls, and he chose them. To him, losing the kingdom was a greater crime than sacrificing those who lived in it. The deepest chambers were sealed. Guards turned to face inward. Servants vanished in the night, and the work began. Some at court learned what the king intended and tried to stop him, and Caer Verre turned against itself. Soldiers of Verre cutting down soldiers of Verre beneath the same banners. In the chaos, a child was taken from the castle. Royal blood, never acknowledged, never marked, never bound by the rites. A servant's door, a hand in the dark, the moon over the walls. That forgotten branch of House Valor would endure long after the ruin. At the height of the siege, Aldrin descended to the Crownheart and began the ritual. The bells of Caer Verre rang out, and the ritual was interrupted. The Crownheart failed to hold one moment. The ancient ring broke apart, and its memory tore in two. The castle as it stood before the catastrophe and the ruin it would become generations later. Two remembered states locked in the same stone. This was the sundering. Generations passed. The road to Caer Verre vanished beneath the forest, and ordinary life abandoned it. But not everything left. Thousands of human imprints remained within the Crownheart, the echoes. Some still remember who they were. Others keep watch at doors that no longer matter, repeating an order long after its meaning died. And sometimes, in windows that fell centuries ago, a torch is burning. The child who escaped did not die. Her line went on, far from Verre. A worn crest, a half-forgotten name, a warning about a castle no one should enter. And from that unbound line came a woman with a claim to the ruin. Valor blood without the completed binding, connected to the castle, yet not imprisoned by it. She came to reclaim a stolen inheritance. She was the uncrowned. Inside, the echoes rose against her, and when they fell, they released the resonance trapped within them, and her blood could gather it. With that power, she could force the castle to choose, and another memory would answer. Rubble gathered itself back into walls. Torches burned where only moonlight had been. She did not travel through history. The castle changed around her. But the castle's two memories did not agree. A door that stood sealed in the past lay broken outward in the present. The wounds were in the wrong places. The stones told a different history. The people of Caer Verre had not been defending their king. They had been trying to escape him. The siege was real, but the catastrophe was Aldrin's. Aldrin did not die in the sundering. He remained, fused with the Crownheart, until king, castle, and memory could no longer be told apart. The last crown. He still believes Verre can be saved, and her unbound blood might finish his ritual. She had come to claim her inheritance. Now she had to ask, "Should this inheritance survive at all?"
